extracted.intended_audience: students, critics, and aspiring novelists interested in literary craft and psychological realism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for writing and judging fiction that emphasizes psychological realism and the analysis of motives, especially in novels. Focus is on characterization, interior consciousness, moral sympathy, and how style and plot serve moral/psychological ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of Motives
rubrics_metrics.description: George Eliot is the greatest of the novelists in the delineation of feeling and the analysis of motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primary criterion: probe why characters act, not merely what they do. Example phrasing on the page: “With her it is not so much that the characters do thus and so, but why they do thus and so.” Use elaborate, painstaking dissection of interior causes and hindrances; track motives through the narrative (Middlemarch, Romola, Tito, Bulstrode).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delineation of Feeling / Character
rubrics_metrics.description: Uncovering certain human lots, and seeing how they are woven and interwoven; delineation of feeling and the analysis of motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create characters whose feelings are precisely observed and articulated; render the mixture of impulses, proud and humble, noble and petty. Use sustained attention to interior life to produce ‘marvellous studies in motives.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction as Means to an End (Novel with Purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: George Eliot belongs to the school of artists who write fiction as a means to an end, instead of as an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novels can be instruments for moral/psychological inquiry; accept that purpose-driven fiction will subordinate some elements (e.g., plot spectacle) to the aim of analysis. Beware that a novel with a pronounced purpose may not maximize pure plot-driven excitement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make Plot, Diction, Situations Subservient to Motive
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot, diction, situations, and even consistency in the vocabulary of the characters, are all made subservient to [the analysis of motives].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize revelation of motive even if it requires altering conventional plot pacing, character-speech consistency, or scenic set-pieces. This is an explicit trade-off in service of psychological truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interior Consciousness / Inside Estimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn from outside estimates of a man, to wonder with keener interest what is the report of his own consciousness about his doings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on characters’ self-report, private reflections, struggles with hindrances and pressures. Present the inner life as the decisive source of meaning for actions rather than external appearance or social estimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological Realism: Probe Complex Motives and Counter-motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Track motives and counter-motives through characters (e.g., Tito’s attempts to slip away from unpleasantness leading to infamy; Bulstrode’s self-justifications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how conflicting desires, rationalizations, and habits interact to produce action; depict moral ambiguity and the gradual explanation of desire into belief. Use lengthy threads of motive development rather than simple one-cause explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of Woman’s Social Lot and Matrimonial Motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Delve into the lot of woman: social promotion in matrimony, causes of match-making blunders, and the mismatch of spiritual grandeur with opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying women, analyze social pressures, heredity, conscience, and limited opportunity; examine why women make matrimonial choices (Gwendolen, Dorothea, Rosamond). Use motive analysis to explain both tragic and comic outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Heredity and Social Background
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrate how heredity and social 'reversion' work themselves out in character (e.g., Brooke pedigree, Puritan forefather in Dorothea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate inherited dispositions, family history, and social background as formative influences on motive and conduct; show lineage and environment as part of motive structure rather than mere backstory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charitable, Sympathetic Judgment; Avoidance of Moralizing
rubrics_metrics.description: She does not say 'served him right' or 'they ought to have known better'—her method is charitable and avoids moral self-righteousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess characters with sympathy and aim to understand rather than condemn; locate coercions and pressures that make people err. Avoid flat retribution narratives and instead present complex, empathetic explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative Empathy (Entering Others’ Experience)
rubrics_metrics.description: The habit of thinking herself imaginatively into the experience of others is central to George Eliot’s method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate an imaginative capacity to feel with characters; use perspective-taking to generate convincing interior life and pathos that resonate with readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of Psychological Observation / Lancet-edged Epigrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Use sharp, epigrammatic phrases and exact observations ('lancet-edged epigrams') to dissect motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ concise, piercing observations that reveal inner truth; these small, precise strokes function like probes into consciousness (examples: 'Examine your words well...it is a very hard thing to say the exact truth').

rubrics_metrics.name: Style Shaped by Purpose; Analytical Phraseology
rubrics_metrics.description: The method of thought produces the form of rhetoric; analytical thinking creates an analytical phraseology—sentences as 'mental landscapes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow the authorial voice and diction to reflect the analytic aim: subtleties, occasional obscurities, and sentences that follow intricate trains of thought are appropriate when probing motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Monstrosity, Romance, or Burlesque; Staying True to Life
rubrics_metrics.description: She draws no monstrosities or monsters, avoiding on the one side romance and on the other burlesque; she keeps to life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep characterizations within believable bounds; avoid grotesque exaggeration or satirical burlesque that undermines psychological credibility. Aim for realistic, life-like depictions shaped by circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair, Unbiased Treatment of Religious Motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze religious motives 'without obtrusive criticism or acrid cynicism' and give fair play to all varieties of religious experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting religious belief or practice, present motives and effects neutrally and analytically; show how religion may be sincere, imitative, or socially inflected without caricature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show Consequences Independently of Repentance
rubrics_metrics.description: Repentance has no more effect in averting or altering the consequences in one case than the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict moral and social consequences as sometimes inevitable irrespective of inner remorse; allow narrative causality to operate without moral tidy-ups that erase complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-study Use of Characters to Illuminate General Truths
rubrics_metrics.description: Use individual characters (Bulstrode, Adam Bede, Dorothea, Tito) as detailed studies that exemplify broader human conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct characters as sustained, specific investigations that collectively map patterns of human motive; prefer cumulative exemplars over abstract theorizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: Pathos Arising from Deep Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The analytical depth produces an atmosphere of sadness and pathos—'To study only the motive...saddens us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that intense psychological realism may create a solemn or melancholic tone; balance with occasional humor/wit to deepen rather than negate pathos (Mrs. Poyser, Mrs. Transome).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of Ordinary, 'Coarse' Lives Alongside Great Types
rubrics_metrics.description: Remember and depict the many common, coarse people whose lives are neither picturesque nor extreme; include them in religion and philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Represent everyday, unromantic lives with care and moral seriousness; avoid focusing only on extremes or exceptional characters when exploring human motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate Depiction of Social Consequences and Public Opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Render how society apprehends and reacts (gossip, exposure, public odium)—e.g., the way Middlemarch gossips affect Mrs. Bulstrode and Lydgate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how public judgment, rumor, and social mechanisms shape characters’ fates; integrate societal forces into motive analysis rather than treating them as mere backdrop.
